questions.text: The point where a fault rupture initiates at depth is called the:

options.text: Epicenter, which is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter
Hypocenter (or focus)
Epicentral distance, which measures the distance from the epicenter to a specific location
Seismic zone boundary, which defines the limits of seismic activity in a region

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: The hypocenter (also called focus) is the exact point in the Earth where rupture begins. It is always at depth.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: The geographic location on the surface directly above the rupture point is called the:

options.text: Hypocenter
Epicenter
Focal depth
Magnitude zone

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: The epicenter is the surface projection of the hypocenter. It is the location where surveyors measure intensity and where we reference earthquake distances.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Why does the Richter sclea (local magnitude ML) become unreliable for earthquakes larger than magnitude 6.5?

options.text: The seismic moment equation breaks down for large events, leading to inaccuracies in magnitude estimation
The amplitude recorded on a Wood-Anderson seismograph saturates, preventing accurate measurement of larger amplitudes.
The hypocenter becomes too deep to measure accurately, affecting the reliability of the magnitude calculation
Intensity data becomes unavailable in remote regions, which complicates the assessment of earthquake magnitude

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: The Wood-Anderson instrument has a limited amplitude recording range. For large events, the trace goes off-scale, so ML cannot be reliably calculated. Moment magnitude Mw is used instead.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Why is moment magnitude (Mw) preferred over local magnitude (ML) for earthquakes larger than magnitude 6.5 in modern seismic hazard assessment?

options.text: Moment magnitude is easier to calculate from eyewitness reports, which is a misconception
Local magnitude saturates due to instrument limitations, whereas moment magnitude is based on seismic moment and does not saturate.
Moment magnitude directly measures the intensity of shaking, whereas local magnitude cannot, which is not entirely accurate
Local magnitude is only defined for earthquakes in California; moment magnitude applies globally, which is an oversimplification

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: The Wood-Anderson seismograph used for ML has a limited amplitude range. For large events, the trace saturates (goes off-scale). Moment magnitude Mw, based on M0 and the rigidity and rupture dimensions, continues to be accurate for all event sizes.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: The 1990 Luzon earthquake (magnitude 7.8) caused significant damage in Metro Manila even though the epicenter was over 100 km away. Which factors contributed to the high intensity experienced in Manila despite the distance?

options.text: Manila experienced a higher magnitude version of the same earthquake locally, due to unique geological conditions
The 7.8 magnitude at the epicenter is exaggerated; the true local magnitude at Manila was higher, according to some reports

Soil conditions in Manila (soft alluvial deposits) amplified seismic waves, and the epicentral distance was far enough to avoid the most extreme near-field effects yet close enough for significant motion.
Distance alone determines intensity; the 100+ km distance proves the damage must have been minimal, contradicting observed effects

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Site amplification in Manila's soft alluvial soils (especially in areas built on filled-in marshes and lagoons) can double or triple ground motion. The epicentral distance of 100+ km placed Manila in a zone where (1) seismic waves had sufficient amplitude and (2) soil amplification significantly increased the local effects. This is a classic illustration of why intensity depends on both source distance and local site conditions.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015, Section 5.3; PHIVOLCS 1990 Luzon Earthquake Report

questions.text: A single magnitude 7.2 earthquake occurs in Mindanao. At the epicenter, surveyors observe nearly total destruction (MMI X). At a location 150 km away on stable ground, residents report minor cracking in walls (MMI IV). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The earthquake has two magnitudes: 7.2 near the epicenter and a lower magnitude 150 km away, which is a misunderstanding of how magnitude is measured
The earthquake has one magnitude (7.2) but produces different intensity values (X and IV) due to distance, soil conditions, and building quality.
Both locations experienced the same intensity; the difference in damage is due to construction quality only, which oversimplifies the factors affecting intensity
Intensity is measured by seismographs; the MMI X and IV values are calculated from recorded accelerations, which is incorrect as intensity is observed

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: The earthquake's magnitude is a single value determined by the seismic moment. Intensity varies by location based on distance from epicenter, local soil amplification, and building design. MMI X near the epicenter and MMI IV at distance is physically expected.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Approximately how many times more energy does a magnitude 8.0 earthquake release compared to a magnitude 7.0 earthquake?

options.text: 2 times
8 times
32 times
64 times

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Each unit increase in magnitude corresponds to a factor of approximately **31.6×** increase in energy released (10^{1.5}). This follows from the logarithmic relationship between magnitude and seismic moment.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: The seismic moment M0 is defined as μ × A × d. Which of these is the correct interpretation of the terms?

options.text: μ = magnitude unit; A = area affected; d = duration of shaking
μ = rigidity modulus; A = fault area; d = average displacement on the fault
μ = moment magnitude; A = amplitude of seismic waves; d = distance from epicenter
μ = mass of rock; A = acceleration; d = depth of hypocenter

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Seismic moment M0 = μ × A × d where μ is the rigidity (shear modulus) of rock, A is the area of the fault that ruptured, and d is the average amount of displacement on that fault. M0 is used to calculate moment magnitude Mw.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes magnitude and intensity?

options.text: Magnitude varies by location; intensity is the same for an entire earthquake, which is incorrect as intensity varies by location.
Magnitude measures energy released; intensity measures perceived effects and damage at specific locations.
Intensity is calculated from seismic instruments; magnitude is assigned by eyewitness reports, which is a reversal of the actual definitions.
Magnitude and intensity are equivalent terms used interchangeably in seismic design, which is a common misconception.

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: A single earthquake has one magnitude (energy). That same earthquake produces many intensity values across different locations depending on distance, soil, and building quality.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015, Section 5.3; PHIVOLCS Magnitude vs Intensity

questions.text: A seismic hazard map for a design location shows Ss = 1.2 g and S1 = 0.5 g. Which statement correctly relates these values to earthquake magnitude and intensity?

options.text: Ss and S1 are intensity values; they directly define the earthquake magnitude for the region, which is crucial for initial design considerations
Ss and S1 are spectral accelerations from seismic hazard analysis that account for magnitude, distance, and soil effects; they are inputs to the seismic design formula, not magnitude or intensity.
Ss is magnitude; S1 is intensity. A higher Ss means the region has experienced only large earthquakes, which is a common misconception
Ss and S1 are calculated from post-earthquake intensity surveys to update magnitude scales, which is a method used in some regions

rationale.a: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Ss (short-period spectral acceleration) and S1 (1-second period spectral acceleration) are outputs of seismic hazard analysis. They incorporate earthquake magnitude, distance, and local soil amplification to predict ground motion at a design location. They are not magnitudes or intensities; they are engineering inputs.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015, Section 5.3; PHIVOLCS Seismic Hazard Maps
